description_full: Newmont Corporation operates as a gold producer. It also explores for copper, silver, lead, zinc, and other metals. It has operations and/or assets in the United States, Papua New Guinea, Australia, Ghana, Suriname, Argentina, Dominican Republic, Chile, Peru, Ecuador, Mexico, and Canada. The company was founded in 1916 and is headquartered in Denver, Colorado.
ceo_bio: Ms. Natascha  Viljoen BEng (PrEng), EMBA | CEO, President & Director | Age 55 | Compensation: $2.8M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 17K people. Revenue per employee of $1.3M ranks in the top quartile among Basic Materials peers, with revenue growing 11%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $417K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $6K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (1/10).
financial_summary: Newmont Corporation is a large-cap basic materials business with a $117.6B market cap on $22.7B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +24% over the past three years and +11% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +4.0pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 3% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $7.3B in free cash flow — roughly 32 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.46× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 50× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 3.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Priced near or above estimated fair value, so the margin of safety has been bid away
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $4.7M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Weakness in commodity prices pressures materials companies
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
39 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Growing faster than most Basic Materials peers — taking share inside the profit pool
Financial quality scores above most Basic Materials peers
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk

sect: Its 51% operating margin runs 42pp above the Basic Materials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 3.92x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 1.4% of sector revenue and 5.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+16.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 221 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 30% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 16% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 49% and a beta of 0.78, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $741.2M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 25% in the 2020 crash, 55% in the 2022 bear market and 61% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $101 (margin of safety -12%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 53%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $74.40 to $142 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Basic Materials peers: EV/EBITDA 6.5 vs 8.3 and P/FCF 16.1 vs 22.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 57% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 6.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 10.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The 20 covering analysts target $135 on average, 20% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 3% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.4%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.37).
It converts 32% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 1.46x.
ROE of 21% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 34pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 0.7% of revenue on R&D and 0.4% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $3.1B (3% of market cap).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 23.9% over 3 years, 14.5% over 5 years and 11.4% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 20%).
At current returns, reinvesting 46% of profits supports about 1.3% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 15.3% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.2x, 13.4% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 46, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 82%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (9 sales, net $4.7M sold).
It returns 2.9% a year to shareholders (2.0% in buybacks and 0.9% in dividends).
The share count has grown 6.4% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, raising it 5.8% a year over the last five.
people: With about 17,500 employees, each generates about $1.3M of revenue, 2.1x the Basic Materials median, and revenue has grown 10.9% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $417K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.8M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
